text: While his army rested and regrouped, Greene opted for another change in his campaign plan:[R]emote from reinforcements, inferior to the enemy in numbers and no prospec[t] of support I am at a loss what is best to be done. . . . In this critical and distressing situation I am determined to carry the War immediately into South Carolina. The Enemy will be obliged to follow us or give up their posts in the State. If the former takes place it will draw the War out of [North Carolina]. . . . If they leave their posts to fall they must lose more there then they can gain here. . . . All things considered I think the movement is warranted by the soundest reasons both political and military.Greene recognized the risk of leaving Cornwallis to march unimpeded into Virginia; he also knew that Cornwallis could remain in North Carolina as well. Greene, however, judged the opportunity to eliminate British outposts in the Carolinas as worth the risk—especially because Washington could send reinforcements more easily to Virginia than to the Carolinas. This last point was borne out by the October 1780 landing of General Arnold and 2,000 British troops at Portsmouth, Virginia. Virginia levies under Brig. Gen. Peter Muhlenberg contained the British until Steuben and 1,200 reinforcements under the command of Maj. Gen. Marie-Joseph Paul Yves Roch Gilbert du Motier, Marquis de Lafayette, arrived in support. Greene decided to move southward in late March 1781, well before he knew Cornwallis’s intentions, yet he hedged his bets

by resting his army at the Deep River until early April. Greene used his time there writing letters to Congress in Philadelphia; Steuben and Jefferson in Virginia; and other officials to obtain fresh levies, supplies, and weapons to replace those lost during the 1781 Carolinas campaign. Cornwallis rested his battered army at Wilmington while he rethought his campaign plans. Instead of resuming his original strategic task of pacifying South Carolina, Cornwallis instead marched his army toward Virginia on 25 April 1781. Once there, Cornwallis fought several engagements but failed to attain his goal of blocking reinforcements and supplies to Greene’s army. Cornwallis entrenched his exhausted army at Yorktown in late September 1781, where a joint Franco-American force compelled his surrender on 19 October 1781. Yorktown was in the future, however, and the present remained uncertain. In the interim, Greene could only advise Governor Jefferson and the Continental forces defending Virginia, while keeping his strategic focus on regaining control of the Carolinas.
citation: Skinner, Harold Allen, Jr. The War in the Carolinas and Georgia, 1781–1782. U.S. Army Campaigns of the Revolutionary War, CMH Pub 71-52. Washington, D.C.: Center of Military History, United States Army, 2026.
title: The War in the Carolinas and Georgia
